Analysis of these attacks further indicates the possible use of AI-assisted offensive tooling, with the interval between initial compromise and fraudulent fund transfer reducing significantly in recent incidents. CSIRT-Fin continues to receive reports of successful attacks, including from NBFCs and fintech entities that had already received the earlier restricted (TLP:AMBER) advisories and had undertaken remediation. The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response. All BFSI entities are strongly advised to treat this campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. Analysis has identified the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools against affected entities including the \"ARTEX\" family of LLM-based, \"PentAGI\" autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system and the \"Cairn\" attack search engine, in addition to the \"CyberStrikeAI\" framework. These tools execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession and adapt their payloads based on target responses. Description Analysis of the reported incidents indicates below attack pattern: Cloud infrastructure of entities targeted including compute, serverless and management services with cloud management services (such as AWS Systems Manager and Lambda) abused to execute commands and deploy malicious files, blending malicious activity into legitimate cloud management channels. Application codebases reverse-engineered by the threat actor to develop tailored exploits; unauthorized API calls subsequently initiated using altered/modified application packages, defeating controls that assumed only the legitimate client application would call the APIs. IP allow-listing bypassed by originating traffic from whitelisted third-party fetcher IP pools (such as content-acceleration and app-store review fetchers); any Internet user can cause such shared fetcher services to fetch arbitrary URLs. Micro-value test transactions (such as Rs. 1) performed to validate unauthorized fund flows before executing large-value transfers. Merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators exploited or abused to move funds. Newly published vulnerabilities exploited as soon as they become public, including file-upload and deserialization exploit chains leading to web shells in PHP and Node.js applications. Cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers targeted, with wallet keys stolen and funds siphoned from cryptocurrency wallets. Large numbers of custom, tailored scripts created on the fly, with functionally identical variants refined in rapid succession; a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development. Alert on token usage from unusual source IPs, user agents or geographies; enforce branch protection, commit signing and mandatory code review on production deployment branches. Replace IP allow-listing of shared third-party fetcher pools with identity-based controls such as mutual TLS, cryptographically signed requests or scoped API keys on dedicated vendor endpoints. Enforce default-deny egress from server segments through allow-listed proxies; unrestricted HTTPS egress was used for command-and-control and data exfiltration. Deploy TLS inspection with alerting on self-signed certificates presented over non-standard ports.
